Editors suggest opposition to engage in constructive criticism, avoid violence
item.description:
Editors of various newspapers have advised the opposition to engage in constructive criticism of the government and refrain from violence on the streets.

Jamaat-e-Islami Secretary General Mia Golam Parwar disclosed this after a meeting with newspaper editors.

The editors held the meeting with Shafiqur Rahman, leader of the opposition in parliament and amir of Jamaat-e-Islami, at his official residence on Minto Road in the capital on Monday afternoon.

Speaking to journalists after the meeting, Jamaat Secretary General Golam Parwar said, “The editors give us suggestions that we oppose [the government]. Criticise it constructively and, when necessary, take to the streets with the people’s demands. But do not destabilise the country by taking an intolerant, destabilising or violent path like previous opposition parties. Some editors sought the cooperation of our amir in this regard.”

Among the newspaper editors who attended the meeting were Shafik Rehman of Jaijaidin, Tasmima Hossain of Ittefaq, Mahfuz Anam of The Daily Star, Matiur Rahman Chowdhury of Manab Zamin, Mahmudur Rahman of Amar Desh, AMM Bahauiddin of Inqilab, Sajjad Sharif, executive editor of Prothom Alo, Dewan Hanif Mahmud of Bonik Barta, Md Mokarram Hossain of The New Nation, Salahuddin Muhammad Babar of Naya Diganta, Shafiqul Alam of Daily Waada, Mustafa Mamun of Agamir Shomoy, Maruf Kamal Khan of Protidiner Bangladesh, Mustafa Kamal of Khabarer Kagoj, Santosh Sharma of Kalbela, Shahidul Islam Chowdhury, executive editor of Desh Rupantor, KM Belayet Hossain of Bhorer Dak, Syed Shahnewaz Karim, acting editor of Shomoyer Alo, Kamrul Hasan, acting editor of Ajker Patrika, Mozammel Haque of Dainik Karatoa, Gias Uddin of Banijjo Protidin, and Shahidul Islam of Manobkantha, among others.

Golam Parwar said Jamaat’s amir outlined the opposition’s role in parliament amid the country’s current situation. He also explained the opposition’s role in parliament and on the streets in resolving the crisis surrounding implementation of the referendum verdict. The meeting also highlighted Jamaat’s role as a responsible opposition party, he said.

The Jamaat secretary general said the party remained committed to breaking with the “bad traditions” of conventional opposition politics and instead helping the government in matters that serve the public interest while protesting actions that go against it. The editors were briefed on this policy, which they also praised, he said.

Golam Parwar said the editors praised the opposition’s role in maintaining stability by cooperating where cooperation was warranted and opposing where opposition was necessary. He said Jamaat’s amir told the editors that the opposition would continue to protest against all wrongdoing and actions contrary to public interests, but that such opposition would be constitutional and constructive.

The meeting also included a question-and-answer session and discussion between Jamaat’s amir and the editors on Bangladesh’s current situation, international affairs, geopolitical developments and relations with neighbouring countries, the party’s secretary general said.

Golam Parwar said Jamaat’s amir raised concerns about the government’s failure to ensure fairness in allocating funds for development projects, allowing the opposition adequate opportunities to speak in parliament and enact legislation, and accepting various notices. He also sought the editors’ cooperation in bringing the truth to light through their journalism.

The Jamaat secretary general further said the editors recalled how opposition parties in the past had destabilised the country through various activities. They believe the government must also act responsibly in this regard, he said.

Responding to a question from journalists, Golam Parwar said editors who could not attend the meeting had called them to explain their reasons for being absent. Jamaat does not believe it has any distance from the media, he said, adding that the party is trying its best to maintain engagement with the media and that Monday’s meeting was part of that effort.

In response to another question, the Jamaat secretary general said the 11-party alliance would not make “the slightest concession” on implementing the referendum verdict. It would be better if the matter were resolved in parliament; otherwise, they would take to the streets, he said.

Besides Jamaat’s amir and secretary general, members of the party’s central executive council were present at the meeting.

item.title: Rohingya crisis: Cox’s Bazar hosts struggle with water, sanitation
item.description:
Nearly a decade into the Rohingya refugee crisis, host communities in Cox’s Bazar are facing a worsening struggle for safe drinking water and adequate sanitation, as poverty, salinity intrusion, climate change and pressure on local services deepen existing vulnerabilities.
The situation is particularly acute in Ukhiya and Teknaf, where communities face cyclones, storm surges, flooding and saltwater intrusion.
For many poor households, shallow tube wells remain an important source of drinking water despite contamination risks, while deeper and safer sources are often beyond their means.
The problem, however, predates the Rohingya influx.
Host communities in Cox’s Bazar have long faced poverty, inadequate infrastructure and limited access to essential services. The arrival of hundreds of thousands of Rohingya refugees since 2017 has added pressure on land, water resources, public services and the environment.
A World Bank assessment found that host populations in Ukhiya and Teknaf are among the poorest in Cox’s Bazar and that the continued presence of the Rohingya population has stretched government service delivery.
It found that 46% of host-community households use unimproved sanitation facilities, compared with 17% of displaced Rohingya households.
A Joint Multi-Sector Needs Assessment also found that 23% of host-community households reported not having enough water for all their domestic needs, while water quality was identified as another concern.
For communities living alongside the camps, therefore, the challenge extends beyond water availability to its quality, reliability and affordability.
Cox’s Bazar’s coastal location makes communities particularly vulnerable to climate-related hazards. Cyclones and storm surges can damage water and sanitation infrastructure, while flooding can contaminate water sources and latrines.
Increasing salinity and limited freshwater groundwater are also making reliable drinking-water sources harder to secure.
Md Nurul Osman, managing director of the Hygiene, Sanitation and Water Supply Foundation (HYSAWA), said coastal communities are particularly vulnerable because of the shortage of safe freshwater sources.
“Due to the lack of safe water sources, many people are forced to consume contaminated water from shallow tube wells,” Osman said.
He said salinity intrusion and the scarcity of freshwater groundwater are worsening the situation. Although deep tube wells are more reliable, their installation costs are too high for many households.
According to HYSAWA’s 2024 annual report, installing a tube well typically costs Tk 100,000–150,000, putting such infrastructure beyond the reach of many low-income families. HYSAWA’s report also identifies climate change, water scarcity and sustainable sanitation as key challenges facing vulnerable communities in Cox’s Bazar.
A HYSAWA-supported community in Ramu illustrates the potential of community-based systems. Its water network is connected to an 810-foot-deep tube well and currently supplies 55 families through a 5,000-litre tank elevated 20 feet above the ground. The project plans to gradually extend access to another 100 families.
According to HYSAWA, more than 100,000 people have benefited from its interventions, including 400 tube wells, 93 solar-powered piped water supply systems and 1,585 improved household latrines.
Each solar-powered piped water system can serve about 30–60 households, providing a more reliable supply while reducing dependence on vulnerable groundwater sources.
Water insecurity is closely linked to sanitation.
The World Bank’s finding that 46% of host-community households use unimproved sanitation facilities highlights the scale of the challenge. During floods, poorly constructed or unprotected latrines can contaminate surrounding land and water sources, increasing the risk of waterborne diseases.
HYSAWA is installing improved household latrines and constructing sanitation facilities on raised platforms in flood- and cyclone-prone areas. It is also conducting hygiene-promotion activities covering handwashing, menstrual hygiene management, food hygiene, latrine cleanliness, water safety and waste management.
The wider WASH response in Cox’s Bazar also continues to focus on both Rohingya refugees and host communities in Ukhiya and Teknaf, with programs covering water supply, sanitation infrastructure, hygiene promotion and solid-waste management.
HYSAWA, established under the Ministry of Local Government, Rural Development and Cooperatives, has worked on WASH services since 2008.
It says it has provided WASH services to more than 10 million rural poor people, worked in more than 1,100 Union Parishads across 27 districts, installed more than 84,000 water points and supported the construction and rehabilitation of more than 1.7 million sanitary latrines nationwide.
Its programs include hygiene promotion, water safety, menstrual hygiene management, food and latrine hygiene, waste management and climate-resilient water and sanitation facilities. It also promotes solar energy, smokeless cookstoves, gender equality and the inclusion of persons with disabilities.
For host communities, however, resilience means more than installing another tube well or latrine.
Water and sanitation services must remain accessible, affordable and functional despite cyclones, floods, salinity and prolonged pressure on local resources.
As the Rohingya crisis enters its second decade, addressing those long-standing vulnerabilities will remain essential to ensuring that host communities are not left carrying an increasingly heavy share of the burden.

item.title: Nine years, many promises, no Rohingya return
item.description:
Nine years after more than 700,000 Rohingya fled a brutal military crackdown in Myanmar and crossed into Bangladesh, not a single large-scale repatriation has taken place, leaving around a million refugees trapped in an increasingly desperate existence with no clear path home.
August 25 marks nine years since the 2017 influx transformed Ukhia and Teknaf in Cox’s Bazar into the world’s largest refugee settlement.
Since then, repeated negotiations, verification exercises and attempted repatriations have failed to produce a sustainable return.
The latest development initially offered another glimmer of hope.
Of the information on 828,824 Rohingya submitted by Bangladesh in phases, Myanmar has verified 426,545 and recognised 308,797 as former residents of Rakhine.
But Myanmar has provided no timetable for their return, saying repatriation cannot begin until the security situation in conflict-torn Rakhine improves.
For refugees who have heard similar assurances for years, another verified list means little without a date and guarantees of safety.
Mohammad Yunus, 48, said: “I have heard many times that the list has been made, it has been verified. But till date, no one has been able to return to their village safely. They are only raising our hopes with the list and then disappointing us again.”
Noor Begum, 36, said: “I am not even sure whether my family's name is on the list. If there is a name but no return date, then this list is of little value to us. We want to return to our country with dignity.”
For the Rohingya, nine years have brought little improvement to the fundamental conditions of their lives.
Families remain crowded into fragile bamboo-and-tarpaulin shelters, with limited opportunities for education and employment.
Healthcare remains constrained, while declining international assistance has increased pressure on food and other essential support.
Insecurity has added another dimension to the crisis, with crime, drug trafficking and human trafficking posing growing concerns inside and around the camps.
Mohammad Salam, 55, said: “We have been waiting for nine years. Now we are hearing about the list of 309,000 people. But if there is no security in Rakhine, a paper list will not change our lives.”
The Rohingya say their conditions for returning have remained largely unchanged: security, recognition of citizenship, freedom of movement and the ability to return to their original communities.
Without those guarantees, they fear repatriation could simply expose them to renewed persecution and displacement.
Bangladesh carries mounting burden
The prolonged crisis has also placed Bangladesh under mounting economic, environmental and security pressure.
Hosting such a large refugee population for almost a decade has affected forests and biodiversity in Cox’s Bazar, while adding pressure on public services, infrastructure and the local labour market.
At the same time, declining international funding has made sustaining the humanitarian response increasingly difficult.
The United Nations and other international organisations have consistently maintained that Rohingya repatriation must be voluntary, safe, dignified and sustainable.
Yet continuing conflict in Rakhine, political instability and unresolved questions over citizenship have kept those conditions out of reach.
As August 25 returns for the ninth time since the exodus, verification of nearly 309,000 Rohingya provides another administrative milestone, but still no road home.
Nine years, multiple lists and repeated promises later, the central question remains unanswered: when will the first meaningful repatriation actually begin?

item.title: MSF president: Rohingya crisis deepening into a health emergency
item.description:
Dr Javid Abdelmoneim , International President of Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) or commonly known as Doctors Without Borders, is a physician who has worked in challenging humanitarian settings, including Gaza and Sudan.
Ahead of the August 25 Rohingya influx anniversary, Abdelmoneim spoke with Dhaka Tribune Chief Reporter Ali Asif Shawon about the health situation in the camps and challenges facing the Rohingya after nearly nine years of displacement.
You visited Bangladesh in 2019. What is the biggest difference you see now?
The biggest change is that the response is no longer in the emergency phase. In 2019, the focus was establishing basic services amid recent violence. I vividly recall seeing no trees, only extensive stretches of plastic sheeting.
There are now roads and semi-permanent homes. While violence remains a concern, the situation has evolved into a health emergency. Restricted movement continues, while non-communicable diseases, mental health problems and gaps in services have increased. Water and sanitation have deteriorated.
Previously, the focus was survival; now it is managing persistent and worsening health problems.
What health problems have emerged since 2017?
About 10% of adults now suffer from NCDs such as diabetes and hypertension. MSF estimates 20% have active hepatitis C, prompting a test-and-treat campaign.
In 2025, MSF conducted 75,000 mental health consultations, mainly for depression, anxiety and psychiatric conditions. About 40% of the population has scabies because of inadequate water and sanitation, causing discomfort and disrupting daily life.
A bigger issue is the lack of hope and control over the future. People remain confined, unable to move freely, and live in limbo.
What concerns you most as a doctor?
Children are arriving at our hospitals with more advanced illnesses and requiring complex care. Referrals of children to higher levels of care have risen 74% in four years, indicating reduced prevention, health promotion and basic healthcare.
It is particularly distressing that one in four people treated for suicide attempts in our mental health clinics is a child.
Can you explain it?
At one Kutupalong clinic, 27% of suicide attempts treated between 2023 and 2025 involved children under 18.
What drives children to attempt suicide?
Reductions in education, food and water services have negatively affected health. These interwoven needs are breaking down, producing negative outcomes and higher interpersonal violence. We treated about 3,500 survivors of sexual and gender-based violence last year.
Imagine the hopelessness, fear, anxiety or powerlessness a child must experience to see ending their life as the only option.
What should be done to reduce self-harm?
All components of the humanitarian response must be in place: food, water, shelter, health and education. Mental health programs are important, but root causes must also be addressed. Most cases are not organic psychiatric illnesses, though a small number may be.
The 75,000 consultations last year highlight the extent of hopelessness.
How are funding cuts affecting healthcare?
Children are arriving later and in worse condition, while hospital attendance is increasing as preventive, public health and primary healthcare decline.
We sometimes have to turn away patients with minor, non-urgent conditions. We’ve had to cap daily patient numbers to maintain quality of care.
Services from other organizations are also declining. Unreliable drug supplies are causing gaps in medication, testing, vaccination and staffing, showing that resources are insufficient.
Are doctors being forced to make difficult choices?
Yes. Patients requiring advanced or tertiary care unavailable in Cox’s Bazar must be referred to Chittagong, a journey that can take eight to nine hours. When facilities are full, few alternatives remain.
Has the crisis become normalized?
We must not accept the normalization of suffering. While death rates alone might suggest it is not an emergency, the statistics clearly indicate a health emergency.
What similarities do you see with Gaza and Sudan?
Every situation is different, but there are similarities: violence, civilians living under extreme pressure, and limited healthcare access. Water and sanitation, prevention and health promotion are key issues in Gaza, Sudan and here. Women and girls are particularly affected in violent or prolonged crises.
What are the implications for children born in the camps?
Children are growing up separated from their cultural roots. Rohingya leaders say adults and elders feel a loss of cultural identity and connection to their lands, which is more pronounced among camp-born children.
Bangladesh has shown remarkable generosity by hosting over a million refugees. But services are declining. Education has been reduced, families have less money for food, and rations are distributed under a three-tier vulnerability system.
Children need safe spaces, education, food, clean water and security, which are not consistently available.
Is safe, sustainable return to Myanmar possible?
No. Returning to Rakhine is currently unrealistic because violent conflict continues. Hospitals have been attacked, including one just months ago and another at the end of December.
A survey of 400 Rohingya found over 85% did not feel safe returning. Safe and dignified return remains important in principle, but it is not currently realistic.
What if funding continues to decline for two or three years?
The situation will worsen. Around 500 Rohingyas have died attempting to cross the Bay of Bengal by boat in recent months. With growing hopelessness, ill health and desperation, that figure could escalate sharply.
MSF is unlikely to reduce its presence soon. There is an urgent health need, and we will continue adapting, providing healthcare and listening to the community.
What are governments and donors getting dangerously wrong?
A long-lasting crisis still causes harm. Bangladesh has hosted over a million Rohingya and sustained the response, but it cannot manage this alone.
Donors and member states must ensure adequate support for health, water, food, sanitation, protection and education.
The community must also be included: “No decision about us without us.”
How sustainable is it for Bangladesh to continue carrying this ‘burden’?
Bangladesh showed leadership at the UN General Assembly last year by bringing countries, groups and donors together around shared responsibility.
We hope Bangladesh will show the same leadership this year as it takes on the General Assembly presidency in September.
Our message is clear: Bangladesh should not handle this crisis alone. Donor countries, regional powers and everyone else must pay attention.
A long-lasting crisis is still a crisis.

item.title: BNP set for broader reshuffle after six-month government review
item.description:
The BNP is preparing for a broader reshuffle in both the government and its party organization following a review of the government’s performance during its first six months in office, with further cabinet changes and party reorganization expected in the coming weeks.
The first major cabinet reshuffle was carried out last Friday after BNP leader Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir was sworn in as president. However, party and government sources said the changes are not being viewed as a final restructuring.
Further changes could be introduced in phases based on the six-month assessment, efforts to accelerate administrative activities, improve political coordination and maintain a balance between the party and government.
Discussions are already underway to induct more ministers and state ministers and redistribute portfolios among several ministries.
At the same time, the BNP is preparing to reorganize its committees from the grassroots to the central level, fill long-vacant posts and restructure committees of its affiliated and associate organizations.
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman announced a 180-day action plan at the beginning of his government.
In line with the plan, the achievements, limitations and activities of different ministries during the first six months are being reviewed.
Some government officials believe last Friday’s reshuffle was an initial outcome of that assessment, although it cannot yet be considered a complete reflection of the six-month review.
The government has not officially disclosed the criteria used to evaluate ministers and state ministers or explained why particular portfolios were changed.
Finance and Planning Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury has said the cabinet’s performance will be reviewed after a certain period and changes could be made if necessary. He also indicated that further cabinet changes may be made.
Three new full ministers and two state ministers were sworn in last Friday, while one state minister was promoted to a full minister.
Another minister’s portfolio was changed, while another was removed from the cabinet and appointed as an adviser to the prime minister with the rank of minister.
Following the changes, the cabinet has 51 members, including the prime minister — 26 full ministers and 24 state ministers.
There are also six advisers to the prime minister with the rank of minister and five with the rank of state minister.
Questions remain over the allocation of responsibilities in several ministries. Some now have political leadership at three levels — a minister, a state minister and an adviser to the prime minister — while several major ministries continue to have multiple portfolios under a single minister.
Government sources said another round of cabinet expansion or portfolio redistribution could take place within weeks.
Agriculture and Livestock, Commerce-Industry-Textiles and Jute, Railways-Road Transport and Bridges, and Shipping are among the ministries where redistribution is being discussed. No final decision has been made on the number of new members or their assignments.
The BNP is also preparing to reorganize its party structure, which senior leaders say had long been geared toward movements and electoral politics and now needs to reflect the realities of governing.
Expired committees at the district, metropolitan, upazila, municipality and union levels, long-vacant posts and leadership disputes will be prioritized.
BNP Standing Committee member Selima Rahman said the party wants to reorganize itself in a new way.
“The party will take initiatives to put the organization in order through discussions with those involved with the party at the grassroots level,” she said.
Acting Secretary General Ruhul Kabir Rizvi said: “Party reorganization is an ongoing process. The party is always in communication with the grassroots, and the next steps will be taken after discussions within the party forums.”
Local government elections, including those to union parishads, upazila parishads and municipalities, have also become a key focus.
Party leaders believe the organization must be strengthened at the grassroots to perform well in these polls. Candidate selection, assessment of local popularity and management of internal conflicts will also be important.
Rizvi said grassroots units would sit together and select a single candidate, with union and upazila leaders choosing candidates with support from district leadership.
BNP Chairman Tarique Rahman has already met grassroots leaders from Rajshahi, Pabna and Chapainawabganj. Party leaders view the meetings as part of preparations for the national council and broader organizational restructuring.
Several central party posts remain vacant, including positions on the Standing Committee and those of senior vice chairman, senior joint secretary general and office secretary.
The party is also discussing whether government and party responsibilities should be separated as some leaders have taken government positions.
Abdul Awal Mintoo, Nurul Islam Moni, Shamsuzzaman Dudu, Asaduzzaman Ripon, Zainul Abdin Farroque and Syed Moazzem Hossain Alal are among those being discussed for vacant Standing Committee positions.
Several leaders are also being considered for senior joint secretary general.
No final decisions have been made on the appointments.

item.title: Abdul Muhith appointed Bangladesh high commissioner to UK
item.description:
7he government has appointed Mohammad Abdul Muhith as Bangladesh’s new high commissioner to UK, according to a notification issued Monday.
Muhith was serving as rector of the Foreign Service Academy. His remaining tenure in that post has been canceled, and he has been appointed as high commissioner on a two-year contract with grade 1 status.

item.title: Depositors protest as Chittagong bank blocks savings withdrawals
item.description:
Hundreds of depositors gathered at First Security Islami Bank’s Halishahar branch in Chittagong on Monday, protesting their inability to withdraw their own savings for urgent needs, with some breaking down in tears.
Police were deployed to prevent any untoward incident as the depositors staged the protest around noon. They left the branch after officials assured them that their money would be returned soon.
Md Alauddin, a depositor and finance secretary of the Sammilito Islami Bank Victims Depositors Association’s Chittagong chapter, broke down at the branch, saying his ailing mother needed urgent treatment but he could not withdraw his savings.
“I cannot afford my mother’s treatment. I am also a heart patient. I need my money immediately,” he said. Association leaders said they had visited various branches across Chittagong over the past 10–15 days and found widespread complaints about difficulties in withdrawing money and accessing banking services.
During Monday’s protest, the association held talks with officials at the bank’s zonal office. The leaders later claimed that the problems of around 66 depositors were resolved immediately, while other urgent applications were sent to the head office on a priority basis.
Around 100–150 depositors from Keranihat, Maheshkhali, Patiya, Anwara and other areas joined the protest. Depositors said they had been suffering for months as they could not access their savings when needed, particularly for medical treatment and other emergencies.
Association Vice-President Sharmin Akter demanded an immediate resolution to the crisis and restoration of normal banking services for depositors.
Meanwhile, a video of the protest at the Halishahar branch went viral on social media, showing several customers crying and shouting over their inability to withdraw money.
A female depositor was heard telling the branch manager, “You want to kill us. We want our money back.” Another woman appealed to Finance Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury to intervene, saying she was a widow from Chittagong and needed her savings returned.
Another customer said she had visited the branch several times but failed to withdraw money. “I have come today to take my money. I am ready for anything. If necessary, I will die right here,” she said.
Kazi Muhammad Sultan Ahsan Uddin, officer-in-charge of Halishahar Police Station, told Dhaka Tribune that police were deployed after receiving information about the protest.
“Many customers were crying and protesting to demand their deposited money. We sent police to prevent any untoward incident, and no such incident occurred,” he said.

item.title: Connecting Bhola and mainland by road
item.description:
By FE

The decision to establish road communication between the geographically isolated island district Bhola and the mainland deserves all-round appreciation. Dependent on only waterway connectivity, mobility of both people and goods is very slow which becomes slower still during inclement weather. The communication gets snapped in time of natural calamities. So, the proposed road link is going to change all such limitations and restrictions. Considering the island's economic potential particularly after the gas find and extraction, construction of a highway connecting Bhola, Barishal and Dhaka is overdue. The envisaged road communication through Hijla and Mehendiganj will drastically slash the travel time between Bhola and Dhaka via Barishal. When the people's mobility accelerates, economy gets a mighty boost. There is no reason why this will not happen in case of Bhola that has so long remained isolated to a large extent. 

In countries like Norway and Japan, even remote islands including those valued for their tourism have been brought under road and highway networks. Bhola may not be a tourist spot but the prospect of its marine resources, in addition to its gas reserve, is quite bright. It stands to be a hub of exploitation of what is called blue economy. So this investment in the proposed highway unfolds limitless possibilities of contribution of Bhola to the country's economy. Even the current status of the island is quite lofty with the haul of different fish species including Hilsha. Sure enough, commercial fishing awaits development not only in the waters around the island but also in the coastal belt in the country's southern districts. Road communications will help develop the marine fisheries and supply chain to the mutual benefits of inhabitants of Bhola and other districts including the capital city. 

Although no details have been furnished about the schedule of feasibility study and undertaking the project, the prime minister's insistence on accomplishment of the task gives a positive vibe. Now that the decision has been made, the ground works should be started as early as possible. Issues like financing of the project and tender floating should be completed within a reasonable time frame. It would be expected that the plan is executed within the term of this government. In a country where even bridges over rivers and canals with the potential of serving people of 10-20 villages are left half or partially done, any project of highway connecting Bhola with the mainland must not be left destined to similar fate. The faster it is started and completed the better. 

Greater emphasis on road communication to the neglect of the railway in defiance of logic has made the country pay heavily in terms of archaic connectivity, environment and costs. The proposed extension of highway connection up to Bhola does not fall under that category of road communication. But it should include an option for railway connectivity in the future when Barishal is brought under the rail network. The merit of developing mass transport instead of pressing into service imported luxurious buses cannot be disputed. But Bhola's case is special and road connectivity will serve the purpose well. Connecting the island district with the mainland will be a milestone achievement.

item.title: Govt must break the cycle of recruitment syndicates
item.description:
By Mir Mostafizur Rahaman

For Bangladesh, the reopening of the Malaysian labour market should be a source of hope. It should also be a test of whether the country has learnt the lessons of the past.

News that only 25 recruiting agencies may be allowed to send Bangladeshi workers to Malaysia has caused concern among recruitment companies and migrant rights advocates. Their fears are not difficult to understand. Bangladesh has already seen what can happen when access to a major overseas labour market is concentrated in the hands of a small number of intermediaries: recruitment costs rise, competition is weakened and migrant workers can end up paying the price.

Malaysia is too important a destination -- and overseas employment is too important to Bangladesh -- for the country to risk repeating those mistakes.

Bangladesh has around 2,500 licensed recruiting agencies. Many have years of experience in sending workers abroad. Restricting access to Malaysia to just 25 agencies therefore raises a basic question: on what grounds are these agencies being selected, and why should the rest be excluded?

If there are legitimate reasons to limit participation temporarily, the government should explain them publicly. The criteria should be transparent, independently verifiable and applied equally. Otherwise, a measure intended to streamline recruitment could instead create a new system of privilege.

The concern is particularly serious because of Malaysia's history as a destination for Bangladeshi migrant workers. Previous recruitment arrangements were dogged by allegations of syndication, excessive fees, irregularities and the exploitation of workers. A small group of agencies and intermediaries was accused of exercising disproportionate control over recruitment, leaving prospective migrants with little choice but to pay high fees to secure jobs.

The consequences were severe. Workers -- many of them from low-income households -- borrowed money, sold land or mortgaged property to finance their journeys. Some reportedly paid far more than the officially prescribed migration costs. A job that was supposed to improve a family's economic prospects could instead leave it heavily indebted.

This is precisely why transparency matters now.

The Malaysian labour market is not simply another destination for Bangladeshi workers. It is one of the country's most important overseas employment markets. For decades, Malaysia has offered jobs to Bangladeshis in plantations, manufacturing, construction and services. A properly managed Malaysian market can provide thousands of workers with regular employment and a pathway to better incomes.

It also matters to the wider Bangladeshi economy.

Overseas workers are among the country's most important economic assets. Every year, millions of Bangladeshis working abroad send money home to their families. Remittances support household spending, education, healthcare and housing, while providing a crucial source of foreign currency for the country.

The importance of remittances becomes particularly clear when Bangladesh faces pressure on its external accounts. Money sent home by migrant workers helps strengthen the country's foreign-exchange position and supports economic stability. For millions of families, meanwhile, remittances are not an abstract macroeconomic statistic but the money that pays for food, school fees, medical treatment or the construction of a home.

Yet the contribution of migrant workers often begins with a considerable financial burden.

The cost of leaving the country can be extraordinarily high. Recruitment fees, travel expenses, medical tests, training and payments to intermediaries can consume a large portion of a worker's expected earnings. When recruitment is controlled by a small number of agencies, the possibility of excessive charges becomes greater, particularly where workers have few alternatives.

That is why the government should resist any arrangement that creates unnecessary concentration in the recruitment business.

There is a difference between regulation and restriction. The government has every right -- and indeed a responsibility -- to ensure that only competent and trustworthy agencies recruit workers for Malaysia. Agencies with records of malpractice should not be allowed to participate. But that objective does not necessarily require creating a closed group of 25 agencies.

A better approach would be a transparent accreditation system. Agencies could be assessed on their record, financial capacity, compliance with regulations, experience, worker-protection mechanisms and history of complaints. Those that meet clearly defined standards could be allowed to participate, while agencies that fail could be excluded.

Such a system would create competition without sacrificing oversight.

The recruitment process should also become far more transparent to the workers themselves. Before leaving Bangladesh, a migrant should know exactly how much the job will cost, who is paying which part of the recruitment expenses, what salary has been agreed, where the worker will live and what happens if the promised job does not materialise.

The government could publish approved recruitment costs and employer information online and require all payments to be made through traceable channels. Digital registration and complaint mechanisms could reduce the role of informal brokers, who often operate in the shadows of the formal recruitment system.

The agreement between Bangladesh and Malaysia should also be judged by what it delivers to workers, rather than simply by the number of people sent abroad.

A successful labour migration arrangement should guarantee that workers receive contracts they understand, wages that are paid on time, safe accommodation, access to healthcare and effective mechanisms for resolving disputes. It should also contain safeguards against contract substitution, forced labour and other forms of exploitation.

The government should make these protections central to its negotiations with Malaysia.

There is another reason for caution. Bangladesh is competing with other labour-sending countries for access to Malaysia and other international markets. If Bangladeshi workers become associated with high recruitment costs, opaque intermediaries and complicated procedures, Bangladesh risks losing its competitiveness.

A more transparent system, by contrast, could become a selling point. If Bangladeshi workers can be recruited at reasonable cost, through accountable agencies and under clear contracts, both workers and employers stand to benefit.

There should be no room for backroom deals or opaque decision-making.

The government must also establish strong monitoring mechanisms after recruitment begins. Transparency at the selection stage will mean little if agencies are subsequently allowed to charge workers excessive fees or use unregistered brokers. Regular audits, worker feedback, public disclosure of recruitment costs and swift penalties for violations should form part of the system.

Most importantly, migrant workers must not be treated simply as a source of remittances.

They are citizens whose labour sustains families and contributes to the national economy. They deserve a migration system that protects their dignity as well as their earnings.

Malaysia has the potential to become an important destination for a new generation of Bangladeshi workers. But reopening that market should not mean reopening the door to the practices that damaged it before.

Bangladesh has an opportunity to build something better: a recruitment system based on transparency, competition and accountability, where legitimate agencies compete on quality and compliance rather than access to political or administrative privilege.

The choice should be clear. Bangladesh needs more jobs abroad, but it does not need more middlemen. It needs higher remittances, but not at the cost of workers being pushed into debt. And it needs a Malaysian labour market that is open and sustainable, not one controlled by a handful of powerful interests.

The lessons of the past should not be forgotten. If the Malaysian labour market is to reopen, it must reopen in a way that puts Bangladeshi workers first.

item.title: Continental Hospital marks 20 years of patient care
item.description:
Continental Hospital in Gulshan marked its 20th anniversary on Monday with an event reaffirming its commitment to patient care.
Chairman Ahmed Ismail Hossain and Managing Director and CEO Malik Talha Ismail Bari inaugurated the event, along with board members, doctors, nurses, directors, and other senior officials.
Hossain said Continental Hospital PLC, one of Bangladesh's leading tertiary-care hospitals and a Joint Commission International (JCI)-accredited institution, is marking two decades of dedicated healthcare service, clinical excellence, innovation and commitment.
He said the hospital has become a trusted destination for advanced and specialized healthcare by combining modern medical facilities, technology, experienced doctors, skilled healthcare professionals and patient-centered service under one roof over the past 20 years.
Bari said: "Over the past 20 years, we have worked as the most reliable institution in the private health sector."
He said the hospital has treated more than 850,000 registered patients, 285,000 emergency patients and conducted more than 90,000 preventive health checkups.
Other milestones cited include more than 17,000 PET-CT scans, 36,000 successful surgeries, 45,000 gastroenterology procedures, 23,500 cardiac surgeries, 75,000 cardiac procedures, 450,000 cardiac consultations and 820,000 cardiac tests.
The hospital also provided radiation therapy to more than 230,000 cancer patients and dialysis services to more than 363,500 kidney patients, according to Bari.
He said: "Behind every number is a patient, a family and a story of trust. These milestones inspire us to remain even more committed to service — hence our slogan, 'We Care More.'"
As part of the anniversary event, a free preventive health checkup was held in the hospital lobby throughout the day for patients and visitors. The hospital also planted 20 trees of different species on its premises.
In the afternoon, the hospital organized Quran recitation, prayers and a milad for the well-being and long life of its patients.

Former Planning Commission member Shaikh Maqsood Ali’s 7th death anniversary Tuesday
item.description:
Tuesday (25.8.26) marks the seventh death anniversary of Dr Shaikh Maqsood Ali, former Member of the Bangladesh Planning Commission and a renowned former civil servant.
Dr Ali started his career in 1957 as a lecturer in Economics at the University of Dhaka.
He joined the Civil Service in 1959 and till his retirement in 1993, served the Government of Bangladesh as members of the General Economic Division and the Industries and Energy Division of the Planning Commission; Secretary, Ministry of Relief and Rehabilitation; Joint Secretary, Ministry of Shipping, IWT & Aviation; Founder Rector of the Bangladesh Public Administration Training Center, Director General of the National Institute of Public Administration, Director, Project Implementation Bureau, and the President’s Secretariat among other distinguished positions
While studying in the UK, he played an important role in mobilizing support for Bangladesh’s independence.
His academic and professional work focused particularly on poverty alleviation, integrated social mobilization, South Asian values and pro-poor development, and he wrote extensively in national and international publications.
His wife, late Dr Sofia Hasna Jahan Ali, was a professor of economics at the University of Dhaka.
His family members seek the kind prayers of relatives, friends and well-wishers for the salvation of his soul.

item.title: How to build a true 2.1 audiophile setup under Tk30,000
item.description:
I used a Creative i-Trigue 3200 for two decades. Not because I am loyal to brands, but because it simply did what it said it would do for the price, and I am not the type to chase upgrades just for the sake of upgrading.
But after 20 years, I wanted something different. Not just better. Something meaningful.
Spend more, get more. It seems the standard of the industry. But this is not true for everything and all the time.
And it is definitely not true for sound systems in Bangladesh right now.
If you are looking to buy a decent setup, you are stuck with two extremes.
Either you grab cheap multimedia speakers that sound like trash, or you get pulled into the “audiophile” black hole, spending thousands just to squeeze out a tiny gain in clarity. Neither works for your ears or your wallet.
It is like someone promising to treat you to a premium box of ice cream, but when you open the box, they hand you a plain block of solid ice. Cold, empty, and disappointing.
The real problem
The sound system landscape in Bangladesh is genuinely thin.
Proper distribution channels barely exist for audio equipment.
Most international brands like Polk Audio, Klipsch, Bose, Harman Kardon, Q Acoustics, or Swan are aftermarket imports, inconsistent pricing, questionable warranty, no accountability.
What you do find through legit channels still does not always solve most basic problems.
And what I find disappointing is that within Tk30,000, there is basically nothing that delivers real clarity and real bass and actual build quality all at once.
Microlab dominates the affordable tier because they artificially boost mid-bass that sounds impressive in showrooms, sounds like garbage at home. Vocals drown. Details disappear.
Thonet & Vander charges premium pricing for ordinary components and basic enclosures; you are paying for their marketing expenses, not hardware.
JBL's portable systems sacrifice stereo separation for portability, but everything crammed into one tube means left and right channels bleed into each other.
Logitech mostly relies on an overwhelming, boomy sub-bass that drowns out clear mid-range vocals and crisp highs.
Yamaha offers genuinely good engineering but sits in a completely different price bracket.
But I found an exception.
The discovery
My purchase rule is simple: whatever I pay, it should return me the equivalent. More is always good but less is not acceptable.
That rule drove every decision. I was not chasing a brand.
I was chasing a specific outcome: feel the texture of a bassline, clear vocal note, hear instruments with actual separation instead of everything bleeding into one compressed wall of sound.
A system that delivers the emotional weight of music, not a hollow imitation of it. A system that does not cheat.
That search led me to the Edifier R1280DBs.
Small bookshelf speakers. Easy to underestimate. At first glance, the spec sheet reads exactly like every other bookshelf speaker in its tier: 42W RMS total power, a standard 55Hz–20kHz frequency response, and a 4-inch bass driver paired with a 13mm silk dome tweeter.
But buried in the spec sheet was something most competitors do not offer: a dedicated subwoofer output port.
That single port changes the entire lifecycle value of the system.
It meant I was not locked into a preset 2.1 package.
I could choose my subwoofer independently based on what I actually needed, not what some manufacturer decided to bundle together.
Understanding why the R1280DBs specifically matters requires looking at Edifier's own confusing lineup.
The base R1280T and R1280 are strictly analog with no Bluetooth and no way to add a subwoofer.
The R1280Ts gives you a sub-out but strips wireless connectivity.
The popular R1280DB gives you Bluetooth but leaves out the sub-out entirely.
The R1280DBs is the only model that handles everything: Bluetooth 5.0, optical input, and that vital subwoofer output. It is not a minor detail. It is the entire reason this setup works.
With the bookshelf speaker decided, I needed a powered subwoofer.
Fortunately, Edifier makes some of the most highly regarded sub-bass hardware in their price bracket.
I am talking about the Edifier T5s, and more specifically, the successor of the T5.
When I first saw the T5s at CES, I knew life is too short not to experience a T5s . Japan's demanding audio community clearly agreed with me, crowned it with the prestigious VGP2025 Gold Award (Visual Grand Prix).
The T5 is solid but T5s is another level of sound and design engineering.
It is a slim, vertical wooden cabinet that is only 170mm wide, yet it packs an 8-inch long-throw driver that goes down all the way to 35Hz.
It delivers a clean 70W RMS of low-frequency performance backed by a high-performance analog front end and a closed-loop Class-D amplifier.
The T5s' slim vertical design is not just aesthetic; it is a deliberate engineering decision for real living spaces. It is not a massive cube that eats floor space. It is not something that fights your room. It is designed to work with it. When you hear them working together, you realize you have not been cheated out of a single decibel.
It might sound a bit strange, but I had to wait over six months for Smart Technologies (BD) Ltd, the authorized Edifier distributor in Bangladesh, to get it in.
About the system
The R1280DBs has a Texas Instruments digital processor inside. This is not a marketing language.
There is an actual silicon brain managing signal flow. When you connect the T5s, it performs what Edifier calls a “digital handshake.”
The bookshelf speakers actively tells their own drivers: everything below 80Hz is not our job. We pass that to the subwoofer. We focus on what we are actually built for.
The result is surgical. The speakers stop straining. They stop vibrating themselves apart trying to produce bass frequencies they were never designed for.
The midrange crystallized. Vocals became sharp and present. Instruments had their own space—drums clearly left, guitar clearly right, bass centered and physical.
When I played the first song that I had already listened to a thousand times, I heard details I did not know existed, textures I had missed for years.
Not because those sounds were not in the track, but because my old system had been burying them under the strain of trying to do everything at once.
The T5s sits against the wall, slim enough that it does not dominate the space. But when the bass hits, it hits.
You feel it in your chest without the room turning into an echo chamber and in a concrete-walled, tiled apartment, that distinction matters enormously.
At Tk16,500, I have not found another subwoofer that competes with the T5s.
Frankly, the price feels criminally low for the performance it delivers.
Pair that with the R1280DBs which nails midrange clarity without sacrificing its own bass presence for just Tk12,500 and the combined value proposition becomes simply unbeatable.
Most competitors force a choice between the two. This combo does not.
Within this price bracket, through authorized distribution channels, this is the best value available.
This is not just my opinion. This is what the market actually offers right now.
Pro tip: The setup
You cannot just plug them in and expect magic. The Low-Pass Filter (LPF) crossover needs to be dialed properly, or you will get muddy overlap that defeats the entire purpose.
Set the LPF knob on the back of the T5s between 80Hz and 100Hz, roughly the 9 o'clock to 11 o'clock position.
This ensures the subwoofer handles only deep bass while the R1280DBs manage the mids and highs cleanly.
If you want a slightly warmer overlap, nudge it higher. If the bass sounds muddy, bring it lower.
Start the subwoofer volume knob at the 12 o'clock position (50%).
Control your overall master volume from your source: Mac, PC, or the R1280DBs remote and fine-tune the sub gain on the T5s until it blends seamlessly without overpowering the bookshelves.
Once you dial this in, the system locks. Everything sits in its own frequency space. No fighting. No compromise. No muddy overlap.
However, file quality matters far more now than it did before. My old system would muddy everything equally: bad files sounded bad, but so did good ones.
This system is brutally honest. Feed them a compressed, low-quality audio file and it will amplify exactly that.
YouTube Premium's audio quality is noticeably better than standard compressed streams.
The difference is immediate and not subtle. Feed the system quality and it returns quality. That is the deal.
Why Edifier
This year marks Edifier's 30th anniversary. Three decades. Worth understanding what that actually means before you assume this is a budget brand doing budget things.
Edifier started in 1996 in Beijing, a group of audiophiles who wanted to democratize high-end sound.
They were the first to mass-produce wooden 2.1 enclosure speaker systems, proving that computer audio did not have to be cheap and tinny.
Then in 2011, they made a move the audio industry did not see coming: they acquired STAX, the iconic Japanese luxury brand that invented electrostatic audio, the global gold standard for high-end headphone engineering.
By absorbing an 80-year-old Japanese acoustic legacy, Edifier integrated elite transducer research directly into their own ecosystem.
That R&D trickles down. When you buy the R1280DBs or a T5s, you are getting technology engineered by the same people who design the Airpulse A300 Pro—Edifier's crown jewel luxury line, built in direct collaboration with legendary audio engineer Phil Jones, featuring ultra-premium horn-loaded ribbon tweeters.
They build the S2000MKII and S3000MKII—universally acclaimed premium audio monitors that command serious respect in high-end audio circles globally.
They do not just make budget gear. They make exceptional gear at every level.
The budget products benefit from the premium engineering. That is the point. That is why Tk29,000 buys you more than it should.
Happy birthday, Edifier. Because of your existence, people like me can finally afford something truly worthwhile.
If you share this ear
If I had more to spend, the Edifier M90 would be the logical next step: better connectivity, premium build, HDMI eARC, Bluetooth 6.0 with LDAC.
But at Tk29,000, this setup does exactly what I asked it to do.
This system is for people who actually care about clarity, bass impact, and separation.
People who have heard a great soundstage and refuse to accept compromise. People who listen to songs multiple times not out of nostalgia, but out of obsession with the detail.
If you are in that category, looking a system under Tk30,000, and want something bought through legitimate distribution channels with actual warranty backing, this is the setup.
Not because it is perfect. Because it is honest.
That is the only reason worth upgrading.
The author is a contributor and tech enthusiast

US plans to revoke up to 200,000 visas of foreigners seeking asylum
item.description:
President Donald Trump’s administration said on Monday it planned to revoke the non-immigrant visas of foreigners who have applied for or are currently seeking asylum status in the US, marking its latest step in a sweeping immigration crackdown.

A State Department spokesman said it was coordinating with the Department of Homeland Security “to identify and revoke the non-immigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently.”

The State Department statement did not specify the number of visas that will be revoked in the process.

The Associated Press put the number of foreigners whose business and tourism visas is planned to be revoked at up to 200,000, which if materialized, would be the largest single mass revocation of visas in US history. The AP cited State Department documents and two US officials.

The State Department will revoke so-called B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026 whose holders have sought asylum or are now seeking asylum, the AP report added. The B1 and B2 non-immigrant visas are issued for business and tourism ​travel.

The visa revocations would not necessarily result in immediate deportation, the AP report said, adding that most of those with asylum cases currently pending would be re-categorized but would lose their status as business or tourism travelers.

Earlier on Monday, Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau alleged on X that the American immigration system “has long been swamped by frivolous asylum claims.”

The State Department said earlier this month that under the Trump administration, it has revoked more than 175,000 visas of foreign nationals.

Trump has pursued an immigration crackdown that includes revocations of visas and green cards and an aggressive deportation drive.He says the crackdown aims to improve domestic security.

Rights groups ​say the crackdown has violated free speech and due process ​rights and ⁠created an unsafe environment, particularly for ethnic minorities, who have raised concerns about racial profiling.

While Trump campaigned in 2024 on a platform of stopping illegal immigration, his administration has also made legal immigration more difficult - for example, ⁠by ​imposing new and expensive fees for applicants of ​certain work visas. The government’s crackdown has faced legal challenges.

item.title: Govt warehouses have fertiliser, problem lies in distribution
item.description:
August is the time for preparing land and planting seedlings for Aman, the country’s main rice-growing season. After planting the seedlings, farmers need to apply fertiliser to their fields in several stages. Naturally, demand for fertiliser is high at this time, but farmers at the field level complain that they are not getting enough.

In some places, farmers are being forced to buy fertiliser at higher prices. However, according to government records, there is no shortage in fertiliser stocks or allocations against demand.

The Ministry of Agriculture says that although allocations are made according to dealers’ demand, they are creating an artificial crisis by not lifting the fertiliser. It is the responsibility of upazila agricultural extension officers to monitor whether dealers are properly lifting and distributing fertiliser.

Farmers allege that a crisis is emerging because government-appointed distributors are selling subsidised fertiliser on the black market outside the designated channels.

The fertiliser is later sold at higher prices in the open market. Over the past three days, four distributors in four upazilas of Rajshahi have been fined a total of Tk 85,000 for allegedly smuggling fertiliser allocated for one area to another area. On 2 August, two distributors in Jashore were fined a total of Tk 10,500 by a mobile court for allegedly selling fertiliser at higher prices.

Farmers failing to get fertiliser as required, prices also higher

Officials of the Ministry of Agriculture say the ministry issues district-wise fertiliser allocation orders every month. In each district, the Fertiliser Allocation and Seed Distribution Monitoring Committee, headed by the deputy commissioner, issues dealer-wise fertiliser allocation orders.

The dealers then lift the fertiliser from designated warehouses. The upazila agriculture officer is responsible for monitoring whether the fertiliser allocated for each month is lifted on time and how much fertiliser is being distributed to how many farmers.

The Ministry of Agriculture says 10,000 dealers are involved in distributing fertiliser across the country. The ministry’s internal investigation has also found negligence at the field level.

Regarding this, Additional Secretary (Fertiliser Management and Inputs) of the Ministry of Agriculture Ahmed Faisal Imam told Prothom Alo, “Field-level agriculture officials are our key operational personnel on the ground.

Although we at the ministry level ensure that imports and allocations are made in the right quantities and at the right time, in some cases negligence by agriculture officials and collusion with dealers are creating the crisis.”

Ahmed Faisal Imam said action is being taken against those found guilty in internal investigations. Three deputy directors at the district level were transferred last Saturday.

A decision has been taken to dismiss an upazila agriculture officer within a few days. Wherever negligence, indifference or collusion is found, action is being taken. Show-cause notices, calls for explanations, withdrawal from posts and, in some cases, dismissal of responsible officials are also being carried out, he said.

Allocations exist, lifting remains low

The district-wise report for August submitted to the Ministry of Agriculture by the Department of Agricultural Extension shows that despite sufficient district-wise fertiliser allocations, the amount lifted is half or less than the allocation in some areas.

An analysis of reports from several districts in Dhaka division shows that 1,876 tonnes of urea fertiliser were allocated to Gazipur for August. As of 20 August, only 800 metric tonnes had been distributed at the farmer level. In Narsingdi district, the August allocation was 2,553 tonnes. As of 20 August, 919 metric tonnes had been distributed to farmers.

In August, the allocation of urea fertiliser for eight districts in Dhaka division was 19,918 tonnes. As of August 20, 8,965 tonnes had been lifted. The same picture was seen in other divisions.

For example, the four districts of Mymensingh division were allocated 31,425 tonnes of urea fertiliser. As of August 20, 9,992 tonnes had been lifted. The four districts of Sylhet division were allocated 9,541 tonnes in August. As of 20 August, dealers had lifted 2,679 tonnes of fertiliser.

Across the country, 279,412 tonnes of urea fertiliser have been allocated for August. As of 20 August, 149,612 tonnes had been distributed.

Last Sunday, following an incident in Bhurungamari of Kurigram where fertiliser was taken away after the door of a dealer’s warehouse was broken, Additional Secretary Ahmed Faisal Imam told Prothom Alo that Kurigram had been allocated 5,875 tonnes of fertiliser for August. As of 20 August, dealers had collected only one-third of the allocation. He said collection of other fertilisers, such as DAP, MOP and TSP, was also much lower than the allocations.

The lifting of TSP fertiliser was similarly found to be lower than the allocation, according to the monthly fertiliser supply and distribution report of the Department of Agricultural Extension. Cumilla district was allocated 1,327 tonnes of TSP fertiliser in August.

As of 20 August, 498 tonnes had been distributed to farmers. The total TSP allocation for three districts in Cumilla division was 2,772 tonnes. As of 20 August, 1,171 tonnes had been distributed to farmers. Four districts in Khulna were allocated 4,337 tonnes of TSP in August. As of 20 August, 2,637 tonnes had been distributed.

State of fertiliser stock

Besides two government agencies, fertiliser is also imported by private companies. The two agencies are the Bangladesh Chemical Industries Corporation (BCIC), under the Ministry of Industries, and the Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation (BADC). BCIC imports urea fertiliser, while BADC imports non-urea fertilisers such as DAP, MOP and TSP.

According to BADC’s August report, the demand for TSP across the country in August is 69,000 tonnes, while the stock stands at 337,000 tonnes. The demand for DAP in August is 89,000 tonnes, while the stock is 327,000 tonnes. The demand for MOP is 78,000 tonnes, while the stock stands at 148,000 tonnes. The annual demand for urea fertiliser is 2.6 million tonnes. For the 2026–27 fiscal year, the stock stands at 482,000 tonnes.

item.title: Failure of repatriation affects Rohingyas, and increases pressure on Bangladesh
item.description:
Myanmar recently said that more than 300,000 Rohingyas living in Bangladesh are former residents of Rakhine. At the same time, Naypyidaw has once again denied their identity as “Rohingya” and brought the term “Bengali” to the fore. Myanmar’s contradictory messages therefore raise the question: has the country’s position on taking back the Rohingyas actually changed, or is it seeking to further complicate the crisis?

Myanmar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said on 17 August that, of the list of 828,824 people submitted by Bangladesh, information on 426,545 had been verified. Of them, 308,797 were identified as former residents of Rakhine. But Naypyidaw did not provide any timeline for repatriation. Instead, it said repatriation would not begin until the security situation improved.

Meanwhile, the “Bengali” controversy has resurfaced. Referring to the Rohingyas by this name is a long-standing position of Myanmar. But as discussions on repatriation resume, questions are now being raised about the political significance of bringing that position to the forefront. On the one hand, Rohingyas are being identified as former residents of Rakhine; on the other, their own ethnic identity is being denied.

The question, therefore, is not simply how many people Myanmar is prepared to take back. If Myanmar remains unyielding over the identity and rights of those it says it is willing to receive, how realistic can that repatriation actually be?

Repatriation announced, but no one has returned

In the weeks following 25 August nine years ago, more than 700,000 Rohingyas fled to Bangladesh. At the time, the equation surrounding repatriation was not nearly as complicated as it is today. The entirety of Rakhine was under the control of Myanmar’s military. International pressure was mounting following the Myanmar military’s horrific atrocities against the Rohingyas in Rakhine.

In that situation, and largely under pressure from China, Bangladesh signed a repatriation agreement with Myanmar barely three months after the influx of Rohingyas began. It was hoped that, through an understanding with the Myanmar government, the Rohingyas could eventually be returned.

That reality no longer exists in Myanmar in 2026. Civil war spread across the country following the military coup in 2021. The military has lost control of various areas. The balance of power has also shifted in Rakhine. The Arakan Army is now one of the state’s principal military and political forces. Amid these changes, Myanmar is once again putting forward figures for repatriation.

Rakhine now under Arakan Army

The biggest change in the old framework for Rohingya repatriation has occurred in the balance of power in Rakhine. In late 2023, the Arakan Army launched a major offensive in Rakhine. It subsequently took control of one military base and key area after another. By late 2024, there were also reports that Maungdaw, along the Bangladesh border, had come under the Arakan Army’s control. As a result, the Myanmar military’s control weakened across large parts of the state, including northern Rakhine.

Although Naypyidaw retains control of some important areas, such as Sittwe, the overall reality in Rakhine has changed. This is where the biggest question over repatriation arises.

The Myanmar government says it wants to take back the Rohingyas. But in many of the areas where they are most likely to return, Naypyidaw does not have effective control. So who will ensure their security after repatriation? Who will administer those areas? Who will guarantee their freedom of movement? And who will make the final decisions on citizenship and political rights? Nine years ago, the answers to these questions were relatively clear. They are not anymore.

New risks for the Rohingyas

The rise of the Arakan Army in Rakhine has created a new reality for the Rohingyas. But it has not brought any guarantee of security. The Arakan Army has been accused of persecuting Rohingyas, restricting their movement, forcibly displacing them and subjecting them to forced recruitment. Similar allegations of forced recruitment have also been made against Myanmar’s military. As a result, there is no easy choice for the Rohingyas. On the one hand, Naypyidaw maintains its longstanding position on their ethnic identity and citizenship.

On the other, the Rohingyas’ relationship with the Arakan Army, which controls large parts of Rakhine, is also complicated. In this situation, repatriation is not simply a matter of crossing the border and returning home. The central questions are who will protect them after they return and what rights they will have.

Bangladesh faces a new reality

The changes in Rakhine are also significant for Bangladesh’s diplomacy. Until now, Dhaka has primarily discussed repatriation with the Myanmar government. But as the power structure in Rakhine has changed, questions have arisen over how much this policy reflects the reality on the ground. In June, Foreign Affairs Adviser Khalilur Rahman told Parliament that Bangladesh was working to establish effective dialogue between the Myanmar authorities and the Arakan Army to create a stable environment in Rakhine.

This signals a significant shift. It does not mean recognising the Arakan Army. Rather, the reality is that it is difficult to completely ignore the side that exercises effective control over large parts of Rakhine when trying to create conditions for repatriation. This reality has already become apparent in some incidents along the border. Bangladesh has communicated with the Arakan Army to secure the release of Bangladeshi fishermen it had detained. In other words, the realities on the ground have already created a degree of contact.

The question is how strategically Bangladesh can make use of this reality. On the one hand, it will have to continue repatriation talks with Naypyidaw. On the other, it will also need to maintain necessary communication with the forces exercising effective control in Rakhine. At the same time, international pressure must be sustained so that the questions of Rohingya citizenship and rights do not fall outside the scope of repatriation discussions. Finding a path toward a solution through dialogue at multiple levels, while safeguarding the country’s interests, will be a major challenge for Bangladesh.

Bangladesh and Myanmar decided in November 2018 to repatriate the first group of Rohingyas. Not a single Rohingya was returned in the first phase. After the two countries failed to make progress, China became involved in efforts to repatriate the Rohingyas. The second attempt, mediated by China in 2019, also failed. The Rohingyas refused to return because conditions in Rakhine were not conducive to their return, including the lack of guarantees of citizenship and security.

At a time when Bangladesh is trying to verify lists and negotiate with Myanmar over repatriation, Myanmar is saying that there is no ethnic group called “Rohingya.”

Myanmar’s strategy on the numbers

Myanmar’s sudden announcement that more than 300,000 Rohingyas had been verified, may have piqued the curiosity of many, but this is not the first time the country has publicised such figures. In April 2025, on the sidelines of the sixth BIMSTEC summit in Bangkok, Myanmar’s Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Than Swe met Khalilur Rahman, then the High Representative to the Chief Adviser of Bangladesh’s interim government. At that meeting, Myanmar initially confirmed that 180,000 Rohingyas had been verified and deemed eligible for repatriation.
The Bangladesh government’s attitude toward such an announcement from Myanmar at the time was essentially to wait for the military junta to put forward a figure. But Myanmar did not say when it would take back those it had deemed eligible for repatriation.

It again said that repatriation would begin once the security situation improved. There was no specific timeline for the return of the Rohingyas. Each time, the process has reached a certain point and then stalled: verification has taken place, but repatriation has not. The picture this time is no different. Here, the distinction between “verification” and “repatriation” is important. Identifying someone as a former resident of Rakhine does not mean that conditions have been created for their safe, voluntary and dignified return.

Old “Bengali” narrative, new questions

Calling the Rohingyas “Bengali” is nothing new for Myanmar. The country does not recognise the Rohingyas among its 135 officially recognised ethnic groups. It has also continued to deny them citizenship rights. But the question now is why this old narrative is being brought to the fore again. At a time when Bangladesh is trying to verify lists and negotiate with Myanmar over repatriation, Myanmar is saying that there is no ethnic group called “Rohingya.” Bangladesh has protested this position. Rohingyas in exile believe it is simply a continuation of Myanmar’s longstanding stance. The refusal to recognise Rohingya citizenship and identity makes it clear, they argue, that the country lacks genuine goodwill toward repatriation.

At the same time, there is another aspect to Myanmar’s recent actions. Its identification of 308,797 people as former residents of Rakhine at least shows that it is not formally denying the issue in its entirety. It is therefore more reasonable to view the “Bengali” narrative not as an entirely new policy, but as a repetition of the old politics of identity. The real question is how much this identity politics is affecting the practical process of repatriation.

* Raheed Ejaz is Special Correspondent, Prothom Alo

item.title: Venezuela quake death toll surpasses 6,500
item.description:
Venezuela's interim government on Monday reported 6,509 deaths from the powerful twin earthquakes that struck the South American nation exactly two months ago.
The magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 tremors on June 24 devastated the coastal state of La Guaira, where at least 190 buildings fell apart.
The previous death toll had stood at 6,438.
Efforts to recover the dead under the rubble are ongoing in La Guaira, where thousands of people made homeless by the quakes are living in makeshift camps.
The interim government has not disclosed how many people remain missing after the disaster.
Authorities say they have provided 335 homes to quake victims, having pledged to provide 4,000 by the end of the year.
